verses.text: After six days Jesus took with Him Peter, James, and John the brother of James, and led them up a high mountain by themselves.
There He was transfigured before them. His face shone like the sun, and His clothes became as white as the light.
Suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared before them, talking with Jesus.
Peter said to Jesus, "Lord, it is good for us to be here. If You wish, I will put up three shelters — one for You, one for Moses, and one for Elijah."
While Peter was still speaking, a bright cloud enveloped them, and a voice from the cloud said, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!"
When the disciples heard this, they fell facedown in terror.
Then Jesus came over and touched them. "Get up," He said. "Do not be afraid."
And when they looked up, they saw no one except Jesus.
As they were coming down the mountain, Jesus commanded them, "Do not tell anyone about this vision until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead."
The disciples asked Him, "Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?"
Jesus replied, "Elijah does indeed come, and he will restore all things.
But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but have done to him whatever they wished. In the same way, the Son of Man will suffer at their hands."
Then the disciples understood that He was speaking to them about John the Baptist.
When they came to the crowd, a man came up to Jesus and knelt before Him.
"Lord, have mercy on my son," he said. "He has seizures and is suffering terribly. He often falls into the fire or into the water.
I brought him to Your disciples, but they could not heal him."
"O unbelieving and perverse generation!" Jesus replied. "How long must I remain with you? How long must I put up with you? Bring the boy here to Me."
Then Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of the boy, and he was healed from that moment.
Afterward the disciples came to Jesus privately and asked, "Why couldn't we drive it out?"

"Because you have so little faith," He answered. "For truly I tell you, if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mountain, 'Move from here to there,' and it will move. Nothing will be impossible for you."
When they gathered together in Galilee, Jesus told them, "The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.
They will kill Him, and on the third day He will be raised to life." And the disciples were deeply grieved.
After they had arrived in Capernaum, the collectors of the two-drachma tax came to Peter and asked, "Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?"

"Yes," he answered. When Peter entered the house, Jesus preempted him. "What do you think, Simon?" He asked. "From whom do the kings of the earth collect customs and taxes: from their own sons, or from others?"
"From others," Peter answered. "Then the sons are exempt," Jesus said to him.

"But so that we may not offend them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish you catch. When you open its mouth, you will find a four-drachma coin. Take it and give it to them for My tax and yours."

context.author: Matthew, writing to a Jewish audience
context.genre: Narrative — the Transfiguration, followed by a healing account, a second passion prediction, and a brief teaching on the temple tax.
context.audience: Jewish-Christian readers, given a momentary glimpse of Jesus' divine glory just as the narrative turns toward His suffering.
context.setting: The unnamed "high mountain" is traditionally linked to Mount Tabor, though many scholars favor Mount Hermon, closer to Caesarea Philippi where the previous chapter's events took place. This occurs roughly six months before the crucifixion, under Roman rule with Herod Antipas governing Galilee.
context.custom: The two-drachma temple tax (v.24) was an annual payment expected of every adult Jewish male to support temple upkeep, based on Exodus 30:13-16 — Jesus' point about "sons" being exempt from a king's tax makes a claim about His own identity before He agrees to pay anyway.
context.timelineImmediate: Occurs about six days after Peter's confession and the first passion prediction in chapter 16 — this mountaintop glimpse of glory comes just before Jesus' ministry turns decisively toward Jerusalem and the cross.
context.timelineBible: Moses and Elijah appearing with Jesus (v.3) represents the Law and the Prophets — the entire Old Testament — visibly affirming Him, while the shining face deliberately echoes Moses' own glowing face after meeting God in Exodus 34:29-35.

translation.meaning: A visible transformation in form — the same root as the English word "metamorphosis," describing a literal, outward change.

occurrences.note: Used only four times — twice for this one event, and twice more (translated "transformed") for the believer's own ongoing spiritual change.

translation.meaning: A present imperative — ongoing, continuous listening — echoing Moses' promise in Deuteronomy 18:15 of a coming prophet whose words must be heeded.
To set right or bring back to a proper state — the expected role of Elijah before the Messiah's arrival, per Malachi 4:5-6.
The noun form of the same word used for Peter sinking on the water in chapter 14 — here explaining the disciples' failed healing attempt.

gospelParallels.note: Mark's parallel account of the Transfiguration, with similar detail.
Luke's version, which adds that Jesus, Moses, and Elijah spoke of His coming "departure" in Jerusalem.
Peter's own later reference to the Transfiguration as eyewitness proof of Jesus' majesty.

otBackground.note: Moses' face shining after meeting with God — the visual precedent for Jesus' transfiguration.
The cloud, mountain, and voice at Sinai, paralleling the Transfiguration's setting.
The promise of Elijah's return before the Day of the Lord, discussed by Jesus and the disciples in v.10-13.

context.sparkNotes: Jesus is transfigured on a mountain before three disciples, His face shining like the sun as Moses and Elijah appear beside Him. "Transfigured" shares its root with the word Paul later uses for a believer's own "transformation" — and the scene deliberately echoes Moses' own glowing face after meeting God in Exodus 34.

commentary.note: Henry reads the moment the vision fades — "they saw no man, save Jesus only" — as the whole point condensed into five words: whatever authority Moses and Elijah carried as prophets, they were willing to see it entirely transferred to Christ, whose silence at "hear him" was itself their consent.

JFB draws a precise distinction most readers miss: the temple tax in this chapter was an ecclesiastical due, not a civil tax like the one debated with Caesar's coin later in chapter 22 — and they argue the whole force of Jesus' reasoning about kings not taxing their own children depends on keeping that distinction clear.

Gill notes that "faith as a grain of mustard seed" wasn't an image Jesus invented on the spot — it was already a known proverbial phrase in Jewish sources for describing something impossibly small in quantity, which makes Jesus' point sharper: even that little is enough.

overview.summary: Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James and John, and Moses and Elijah appear. A voice from the cloud says to listen to Him. He heals a boy the disciples could not, predicts His death again, and pays the temple tax with a coin from a fish.

history.t: Every adult Jewish man paid two drachmas a year toward temple upkeep.
Capernaum lay in Herod Antipas' Galilee, where tolls and taxes were collected.

customs.t: Peter's offer of shelters recalls the booths built at the Feast of Tabernacles.
A stater was a silver coin worth four drachmas, enough for two men's temple tax.

archaeology.t: A church on Mount Tabor honors the Transfiguration, though the Gospels name no mountain.
Tyrian silver coins, like the one in the fish, are common finds in Jerusalem.

overview.discussion: At the Transfiguration a voice said, "Listen to Him." What do you think the disciples most needed to hear?
overview.book: The first Gospel · 28 chapters. Written to show Jesus as the Messiah the Old Testament promised.
overview.author: Matthew
